Map Configuration and Styling

Source: vignettes/articles/r-docs/map-configuration.Rmd
map-configuration.Rmd

Mapbox Maps vs Geo Maps

Plotly supports two different kinds of maps:

  1. Tile maps are tile-based maps drawn with MapLibre. If your figure is created with one or more add_scattermap(), add_choroplethmap() or add_densitymap() traces, the map layout object (go_map()) in your figure contains configuration information for the map itself.
  2. Geo maps are outline-based maps. If your figure is created with add_scattergeo() or add_choropleth(), the geo layout object (go_geo()) in your figure contains configuration information for the map itself.

This page documents Geo outline-based maps, and the Map Layers documentation describes how to configure tile-based maps.

Note: Every configuration option here is equally applicable to non-empty maps created with add_scattergeo() and add_choropleth().

Physical Base Maps

Plotly Geo maps have a built-in base map layer composed of “physical” and “cultural” (i.e. administrative border) data from the Natural Earth Dataset. Various lines and area fills can be shown or hidden, and their color and line-widths specified. In the default template, a map frame and physical features such as a coastal outline and filled land areas are shown, at a small-scale 1:110m resolution:

library(plotly.core)
g <- go_geo(showland = TRUE, landcolor = "#e5ecf6")
fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Here is a map with all physical features enabled and styled, at a larger-scale 1:50m resolution:

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  scope = "world",
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "LightGreen",
  showocean = TRUE,
  oceancolor = "LightBlue",
  showlakes = TRUE,
  lakecolor = "Blue",
  showrivers = TRUE,
  rivercolor = "Blue",
  resolution = 50
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Disabling Base Maps

In certain cases, such as large scale choropleth maps, the default physical map can be distracting. In this case the visible attribute of go_geo() attribute can be set to FALSE to hide all base map attributes except those which are explicitly set to true. For example in the following map we hide all physical features except rivers and lakes, neither of which are shown by default:

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  scope = "world",
  visible = FALSE,
  showlakes = TRUE,
  lakecolor = "Blue",
  showrivers = TRUE,
  rivercolor = "Blue",
  resolution = 50
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Cultural Base Maps

In addition to physical base map features, a “cultural” base map is included which is composed of country borders and selected sub-country borders such as states.

Note and disclaimer: cultural features are by definition subject to change, debate and dispute. Plotly includes data from Natural Earth “as-is” and defers to the Natural Earth policy regarding disputed borders which read:

Natural Earth Vector draws boundaries of countries according to defacto status. We show who actually controls the situation on the ground.

To create a map with your own cultural features please refer to our choropleth documentation.

Here is a map with only cultural features enabled and styled, at a 1:50m resolution, which includes only country boundaries. See below for country sub-unit cultural base map features:

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  scope = "world",
  visible = FALSE,
  showcountries = TRUE,
  countrycolor = "Purple",
  resolution = 50,
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Map Projections

Geo maps are drawn according to a given map projection that flattens the Earth’s roughly-spherical surface into a 2-dimensional space.

The available projections are 'equirectangular', 'mercator', 'orthographic', 'natural earth', 'kavrayskiy7', 'miller', 'robinson', 'eckert4', 'azimuthal equal area', 'azimuthal equidistant', 'conic equal area', 'conic conformal', 'conic equidistant', 'gnomonic', 'stereographic', 'mollweide', 'hammer', 'transverse mercator', 'albers usa', 'winkel tripel', 'aitoff' and 'sinusoidal'.

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  projection = go_geo_projection(
    type = "orthographic"
  ),
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig
library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  projection = go_geo_projection(
    type = "natural earth"
  ),
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Map projections can be rotated using the rotation of go_geo_projection(), and maps can be translated using the center of go_geo(), as well as truncated to a certain longitude and latitude range using the range of go_geo_lataxis() and go_geo_lonaxis().

The map below uses all of these attributes to demonstrate the types of effect this can yield:

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  projection = go_geo_projection(
    rotation = go_geo_projection_rotation(lon = 30, lat = 30, roll = 30)
  ),
  center = go_geo_center(lon = -30, lat = -30),
  lonaxis = go_geo_lonaxis(range = c(0, 200)),
  lataxis = go_geo_lataxis(range = c(-50, 20)),
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Automatic Zooming or Bounds Fitting

The fitbounds attribute of go_geo() can be set to locations to automatically set the center and latitude and longitude range according to the data being plotted. See the choropleth maps documentation for more information.

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  fitbounds = "locations",
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(
    mode = "lines",
    lat = c(0, 15, 20, 35),
    lon = c(5, 10, 25, 30)
  ) |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Named Map Scopes and Country Sub-Units

In addition, the named “scope” of a map defines a sub-set of the earth’s surface to draw. Each scope has a default projection type, center and roll, as well as bounds, and certain scopes contain country sub-unit cultural layers certain resolutions, such as scope="north america" at resolution=50 which contains US state and Canadian province boundaries.

The available scopes are: 'world', 'usa', 'europe', 'asia', 'africa', 'north america', 'south america'.

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  visible = FALSE,
  resolution = 50,
  scope = "north america",
  showcountries = TRUE,
  countrycolor = "Black",
  showsubunits = TRUE,
  subunitcolor = "Blue",
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

The "usa" scope contains state boundaries at both resolutions, and uses the special 'albers usa' projection which moves Alaska and Hawaii closer to the “lower 48 states” to reduce projection distortion and produce a more compact map.

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  visible = FALSE,
  resolution = 110,
  scope = "usa",
  showcountries = TRUE,
  countrycolor = "Black",
  showsubunits = TRUE,
  subunitcolor = "Blue",
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Graticules (Latitude and Longitude Grid Lines)

A graticule can be drawn using the showgrid of go_geo_lataxis() and go_geo_lonaxis() with options similar to 2d cartesian ticks.

library(plotly.core)

g <- go_geo(
  lonaxis = go_geo_lonaxis(showgrid = TRUE),
  lataxis = go_geo_lataxis(showgrid = TRUE),
  showland = TRUE,
  landcolor = "#e5ecf6"
)

fig <- go_figure() |>
  add_scattergeo(mode = "markers") |>
  update_layout(geo = g)
fig

Reference

See go_geo() for more information and chart attribute options!
